paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The London Underground, often called the Tube, is the oldest underground railway in the world. It opened in 1863, when steam trains carried passengers between Paddington and Farringdon, a distance of about six kilometres. On the first day, around thirty thousand people used it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Today the Tube has eleven lines and two hundred and seventy stations, and it carries more than a billion passengers a year. Each line has its own colour on the famous map, which was designed in 1931 by Harry Beck, an engineer who worked for the railway. His map showed the stations in straight lines and did not show real distances, but passengers found it much easier to use, and nearly every city has copied the idea since.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Travelling by Tube is fast, but it is not always comfortable. At busy times, trains are crowded, and the air in the tunnels can be hot, especially in summer. Some deep lines are among the hottest places in London because the tunnels are small and trains give off heat. To keep passengers cool, the company is trying new ideas, such as cooling systems under the platforms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many visitors use an Oyster card or a contactless bank card to pay. The price depends on the zone, and a journey in the centre is cheaper outside the busiest hours. There is also a daily limit, so that frequent travellers never pay more than a fixed amount in one day. Children under eleven travel free when they are with an adult.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone knows that the Tube is only part of the story. Some stations are famous for their design, and a few, such as Canary Wharf, look more like modern art galleries than train stations. Others are no longer used. They are known as ghost stations, and one of them, Aldwych, has been used as a film set. Walking tours let visitors explore these places once a year.
